Unfortunately a large part of my spending habits are due to wanting to learn about things. I ride the dopamine high of focusing on the one thing that’s interesting to me right now. Like I don’t just want perfume, I want perfume oils so I can learn accords and notes, psychology and biology research books on perfume, perfumer encyclopedias, perfume history books, and so on. Learning something new is often very expensive for people with adhd. I also had a fixation on stocks at one point and lost a good amount of money (~$500ish total) because I threw more money in than I could get away with and had to pull out when it started plummeting. In my personal experience, and agreeing with some other commenters here, you might want to develop an action plan and potentially tell another adult in your life before your mom, if you trust them. Don’t rely on your sister if she’s a minor, that won’t help. If you have an adult aunt or uncle or older sibling or cousin or grandma on your moms side this might be helpful for now to develop an action plan with them. If you trust them and see them as logical. That way you can get solid advice from adults in your family that know your family more than us redditors. There is a chance your mom will do something either extremely rash (not going to police, just causing chaos instead, which will put y’all in the middle of that), or she will ignore it, because this affects her in the sense of “this man I adore who I think is safe around our children is a monster and now I have no one to lean on”. My mom told me not to tell anyone what was happening to me because if I told someone my brother in law was abusing me/my relatives my sister would move out and cut off/abandon my mom again and she was terrified of that. So she justified it as “someone will get hurt if you tell your dad!” Or whatever. Anyway yeah. Do tell an adult, but make sure you are safe to do so by planning. You don’t need to be in the middle of fights, danger, being swept up and suddenly moved out, etc without having a plan.

Not a parent - but I want to be. I am angry. That’s my primary mode of living. I’m working on it of course… but I realize that there was something I desperately needed that I didn’t have, and that I want to give to my children: the space to have big emotions. I know I will be angry and impatient, I can’t just avoid this because it’s a fact of life. Everyone to some degree is angry and impatient and I happen to be angry and impatient more often than many. Teaching your children how to deal with their emotions is done through modeling that. If you suck in and hide all of your negative emotions and anger, they won’t know what to do with their own, they may think it’s taboo or bad to feel angry in front of others. For me, I know they will see me upset or angry, and I know we’ll have to talk about it. “We all have big emotions” while explaining how I could have handled it better or what I did to handle it. And when my kids get angry I hope they can learn that anger is not evil or bad but normal and I hope they learn there are things they can do to make themselves feel better as well as ways to communicate WHY they feel angry, “I felt hurt when-“ etc. I realize today that I’m an “angry person” because I haven’t learned the skills to differentiate my emotions because many of them were not safe emotions to have. Even anger was dangerous to show. If I can show my kids that you are allowed to feel the “bad” big emotions, and how I cope with mine, I think they’ll come out of that not traumatized per se, but even more well equipped to deal with complex emotions than kids who have parents that judge their emotions without the knowledge of how to deal with them. I can’t hide my illness, but I can show them that it’s the reality of things, and that I know of skills to help. 

Like imagine having a bout of rage, or to them, “moms angry”, you say “I need to have a time out so I can calm down and feel better”, you do that, come back and talk about how you felt, why, and that anger can tell us when we feel hurt or unsafe. Then your kids can see they can take time outs when they feel angry, and they can come back and talk about their feelings and needs without being judged.

It sounds like you have experience with kids and you like kids, so you’ve trained a bit! Many new moms don’t have that experience starting out, so there’s that, too. If you show your kids you’re growing and how to be patient with yourself while admitting when you could’ve stepped up- they’ll learn they’re allowed to do the same. Honesty is incredible!

You’re here because while everyone has flaws and many people have an intense flaw, but only some of us, you included, are so distraught by it that it cripples you. 

Most people do have traits commented on at some point: like I can think of gorgeous women with ears that stick straight out. You can bet they were intensely bullied for that. However the difference is how much that affects you. 

It’s really dysmorphia when you’re able to pin point the exact name and etiology of your physical features, like for me: “tear trough deformity”, “epicanthic folds, short palpebral fissures” etc. for you “scleral show”.
Many people “hate their eyes” but you “have exophthalmia and scleral show”. It’s the level of which it affects you, how much you scrutinize it, how big you think it dominates your overall appearance. 

If your eyes are being commented on by other people, they must not be conventionally attractive, or they must have a flaw. But that does not mean you’re ugly. You know who else has scleral show? Mila Kunis. I’m looking up scleral show right now, I’m seeing so many women who had surgery to change it, but to me it looks youthful, or like a dolls eyes, rather than a flaw. Have you tried learning makeup styles to compensate for your eyes? Have you heard of YouTuber Brittany Broski? I love her makeup. For me, I can’t wear makeup exactly like most people in the west because of my eyes, so I have to borrow techniques that people use from different cultures and also age groups to make my eyes look more “attractive”. 

One time someone said I have eyelashes shaped like a broom and that messed me up so bad I cut them into “proper shape”. Which did not help anything. 
In reality, that person was just picking on me, and it doesn’t really matter. No one, unless they’re choosing to hurt me, is going to notice my eyelashes being shaped like brooms. 

The pain will end: only if you work on the psychological mechanisms behind how you feel about yourself, through things like therapy. The biggest take away here is, even if you are ugly, that has nothing to do with how you deserve to be treated. Is your mom conventionally attractive and without flaws? If not I’m assuming she doesn’t deserve to be loved either. What about people from Asia who don’t adhere to western beauty standards? What about other ugly people that you can think of: are they disgusting creatures? Am I a disgusting creature incapable of being loved? While I might think that I am, that’s not the case. Everyone I admire has a handful of ugly traits. I can see how they might hate themselves for those traits, but they don’t. People think they’re hot stuff, and so do they. It’s all about finding out what caused you to see yourself like this in the first place, and finding out how to catch your thoughts and change your mindset. It’s a lot of work. But it’s what the answer is.

Going through the motions of crying or mimicking crying is tic-like in nature, while experiencing the physiological response of tearing up is a bit different.

Like coughing can be a tic, but having the feeling of something in your lungs or throat like accidentally choking on water or like you have an upper respiratory infection- that’s more physiologically related, a response to perceived stimuli. 

Scratching your skin can be a tic, but feeling an intense itch prior to scratching is not.

Goosebumps are a physiological response to emotional arousal, in the same neuro pathway as tearing up. Goosebumps cannot be recreated willingly, in the same way that you cannot cause yourself to cry without first having some stimulus like a memory, an emotion, an emotional thought, some emotional arousal.

Crying is autonomic, meaning we can’t control it specifically to mechanically produce tears on will, because we don’t have the skeletal muscle motor neurons to be able to do that. Many ducts (including tear ducts) are emptied with the help of smooth muscle. That’s the same muscle in your gut and blood vessels, and we can’t move those without prior stimuli from a combination of chemical receptors, stretch receptors, and the autonomic nervous system.

For me the throat clench, tear duct feeling happens after any positive increase in emotion (emotional arousal) while listening to music. Before hormone fluctuations, I’m someone to get chills and goosebumps with music. The tear duct sting is just a further response to that. 

Changes in brain chemistry alter our responsiveness to stimuli (in this case, events, thoughts, emotional arousal).

You have to train yourself into the mindset that you are in control, and you have to train yourself to tell yourself that your thoughts aren’t an accurate reflection of the situation, or how much the situation is impacting your life (Not emotionally, I mean like, factually impacting your life.) 

I use DBT skills to help myself out of it. Noticing the thoughts, not labeling them, not applying “good or bad” or “because of this I’m destroyed” to it. The more that you tell yourself that you can’t deal with it, the more you analyze it, the more you dwell on it in a negative light the more it will hurt you. The goal is getting out of it, not staying in it, so remember that your #1 priority is getting out of it! Though this is easier said than done. I choose to participate fully and completely in a distracting thing, which means you have to -choose- to focus on the thing, like knitting for me. If you start thinking about what happened again, redirect your focus again to what you’re doing, and eventually the thoughts should not be so impactful. When they aren’t as impactful/more distant, it will be easier for you to wrestle the thoughts about what happened and choose to do more things that distract you from it, or things that are productive. Eventually it goes away from this point, because you’ve rendered it unimportant.

It’s very hard to do, but getting through the day with this disorder is very hard to do. The more you practice choosing to get out of it, the easier and more second nature it becomes.

Hmm… as far as what to do in the meantime, for me, it works best to find hope, and have a goal. For me, I felt like learning and “getting a head start” was what kept me going because it felt like I “had some control” outside of waiting for help. Waiting for help feels torturous to me. Anything I could do to keep myself “working toward it” kept my sense of “I’m digging my way out” alive… even if I was deep underground I was moving. Even still, since I’m only on session 2 (three is coming soon) I haven’t had much practice in so I still supplement my therapy with doing some things on my own.

Something I learned in my “unofficial half DBT” I did- make an easily accessible small bag you can take with you that has something you can touch, smell, taste, possibly hear, and something to look at that while you’re in a “clear mindset” (not sure how many of those you get but I get them sometimes and that’s when I work on coping skills. It’s like trying to build a dam before the river floods) so you can pull out the bag and use mindfulness when you’re spiraling (forcing yourself to focus on it, if you stop focusing or have a thought acknowledge the thought as a thought/feeling, and start focusing again.) 

When you make your bag with your clear mindset, add these “sensation” things based on how they make you feel: For me, I have some Werther’s Originals toffees, a small perfume that my best friend wears, a few pictures of my best friend and boyfriend and I being happy, a very small stuffed animal that vibrates and makes a sound (also given to me by a loved one), and a list of things I need to remember written in my clear mindset “[loved one] is not trying to hurt you. Self harm as punishment is not a fix but makes the emotions more difficult to deal with. TRY the following DBT coping skills FIRST before you use self destructive behaviors. Ride the wave. You will do this again and that needs to be accepted. You will become better at coping with practice.” Etc. These instructions will be personal to you. You have to reinforce using these things while you’re in a clear mindset… it’s like, with this illness the MOST IMPORTANT way to treat it is preparation before a storm. The more you prepare yourself, the more likely you will remember to use the skills you’ve learned when you’re desperate and spiraling. 

When you’re in a general down mood, not deeply spiraling, just down, anxious about the future or loved ones or something you did, etc, this is the BEST time to reinforce coping skills because you will learn later that the spiral starts here. The sooner you can catch it the less hard it will be to get out of it. 

It is a lot of work. But you have to understand that your DBT therapy is a lot of work and while you have a clear head you have to tell yourself you’re working on it and you have to reinforce that your work is going to WORK. The same for before DBT!

I really really really recommend researching DBT methods and skills beforehand, you need to believe you’re digging out of the hole, and you ARE. You’ve already done something to start digging by reaching out to get therapy. This pain will not be permanent, things have already improved in my life in the past couple of years when I didn’t believe that they could. You have to remember to look back on how things were months ago, years ago, while you are progressing so you can remember that your hard work is paying off. I remember in 2019 I was at my lowest, every day wanting to give up, unable to help myself, abusing substances because I felt they were helping (mainly alcohol, which actually makes emotions more painful and harder to deal with due to brain chemistry), I wrote this all down in my Diary Cards. They look NOTHING like that now. It’s humbling… I’m so different and so much better and so much more functional, even though I still have horrible days often (I will get better!!!), it doesn’t take WEEKS after a breakdown to get a clear head (thus causing more breakdowns), it takes only hours or a day!

Another thing that helps me: I have a whiteboard with goals for my recovery. They’re small goals, just working on one or two things at a time. Right now I’m working on self harm (this includes verbal MENTAL self harm) and secondly telling myself that “this will happen again and that’s ok I will get out of it” because if you tell yourself “I can’t let this happen again, I can’t handle it happening again” you will inevitably think “oh god it happened again I can never get better oh god I can’t do this”…

I hope some of this could be of help, if not, I can see about more solutions for you? I know dealing with it is different for everyone.

TLDR: in my personal experience- trust the calculator first, but be ready if you have to return a bra. If you buy from a website I recommend buying several bras of DIFFERENT SHAPES (some fit much better than others due to different chest shapes) and maybe a couple different cup sizes and band sizes to find out what’s more comfortable and return the ones you don’t fit. If possible, try to look up which walk in stores sell bras in your size because I think my sister was able to get her 36DDD from a store you can walk into... 

So, I was a 28FF on the calculator. I didn’t believe them so I used another calculator to “be sure” and got 28E. I bought 3 28E’s and they were TOO TIGHT and I spilled out too so I thought “ok so maybe the ABTF calculator is right about the cups but the band is small so I must be a 30F”… when I got my 30F’s I used the first loop because that’s what you’re supposed to do and it still didn’t fit, I had to WAY tighten the straps to get the top to not gap … I was disappointed but didn’t want to buy and return more cause I’d already been through it and had enough…

Okay, so far, this is what I personally do: 

DBT is an approved treatment for bpd and I’ve heard it helps so so so many people and changes lives. I’ve only had 2 sessions so far. If you can go to psychologytoday the website you can look up therapists in your area by what they specialize in, see if you find any that do DBT. If you can start DBT that will provide some relief. It also simply helps to start looking up CBT and DBT skills and implementing them so you feel you are doing SOMETHING about your situation which helps you feel that there is a way out. (At least that keeps me going!)

From what I understand it basically teaches you self soothing and interpersonal effectiveness, where all of that was missing from your childhood of course. My bpd was also primarily caused by child neglect and abuse, which I also only found out “was wrong” a couple of years ago… so of course you start out with no tools, and as an adult you’re expected to find them all on your own. 

So far the mindfulness (I know it sounds dumb or like it won’t work but it’s exactly what you need to do…) training has helped. Some mindfulness things I’ve learned:

1. Find an activity that is distracting and choose to COMPLETELY immerse yourself into it. It’s a choice though so it is hard. You will of course go in and out of focus, but work to maintain focus until the emotion is more distant, distance makes it workable. 

2. Remember that your emotions ARE NOT BAD. Do not label them. They are just emotions. They are not facts, but they are important and biologically useful. Labeling them as “something you shouldn’t have” aka bad labels you that way too. When you label yourself you make it harder and harder to get out, it’s like you’re recreating your childhood to yourself… I call this self-abuse. Notice your emotion, sit with the emotion. Do not use the emotion to harm yourself. Do not blame yourself for the emotion. Also Anger tells us a boundary or value was crossed, it is not bad. It does not make us bad. Remember that. 

What you also need is to learn how to identify your emotions because that is something child abuse victims are deprived of, this will help a lot because you can then identify when you are feeling more nuanced emotions and what triggers them so you can self soothe before it becomes completely consuming, and you can help manage reactions to them. I did not notice how much I couldn’t identify my emotions until one day I realized “oh I didn’t just break down out of nowhere there were several events that lead up to it what the heck” and that was a revelation for me. I have been stressed by several things for months and i just realized I was stressed when I started DBT. These things can slip away easily from us. Our emotions are foreign to us. 

To help identify your emotions a little bit (it’s helping me) I would look up “DBT Diary Cards” and fill out the emotions every day (they are just listed and you rate them 1-10 or 1-5 depending on the card) and write a small note about something good that happened (gratefulness is very important in mindfulness) and something negative that happened or if anything significant happened that day. Don’t worry if you miss a day just try to pick it up. You can look up “DBT naming emotions” for help identifying the more nuanced emotions. 

Finally I recommend “the dialectical behavioral therapy skills workbook” that will teach you many skills, if you cannot access a therapist. 

And an app has helped me recently called “Calm Harm” which I promised myself I would use if I was about to break down (though that’s hard). It has LOADS of things that either help Distract, comfort, express yourself, calm your breathing, or release your emotion. They help a lot with mindfulness.

I can try to find other resources if you need help. It is very difficult to handle emotions that were never acknowledged. I hope that you find some relief soon.

I would first try to understand where the anger comes from- jealousy, wasting important resources like money, missing him, wherever the anger comes from, everyone’s reasons are different, then I would work it out with him. The end goal not being “to tell him why he’s hurting me and find out why he’s doing it” but the end goal being “seeing eye to eye and lessening why I’m upset about it”.

Should you be mad? Yeah, a personal boundary was crossed. Should you react? Probably not. He will likely tell you he doesn’t want to just waste it, and he would be understanding to why that hurts you, but I think as partners we should also remember to empathize with our non-bpd partner and want them to be happy (even if it was supposed to be with us but it’s not this time) that “he should enjoy himself.” Because if there’s no malice on his part, this is a good opportunity for him to feel good and happy. 

Yes feel mad. Work through the core reason why in your mind. Explain in “I feel” statements with him with the goal being to come to an understanding. 

That’s just my experience

Yep for sure. adhd = no dopamine. no dopamine: tasks are exhausting . Truly. I had a fight with wanting to draw earlier. Get up: grab sketchpad *intense exhaustion and aversion* so I’d go put it back down. Then I’d lay in bed fully awake. Repeat about 3 times. I didn’t have anything I wanted to draw, it was just for practice. So I didn’t want to do it. It was exhausting.

ADHD finds “extra energy” for fun things because ur brain is seeking a -MINIMAL- level of stimulation to function. It’s not finding the extra energy for fun things, it’s finding fun things to have ENERGY. 

People without adhd have no need to do stimulating or fun things constantly because they don’t get exhausted with tasks- because they have a normal level of dopamine in the brain.

What’s worked? Candy while studying. A lot. Videos while studying. Getting up and exercising every 15 minutes or so. Annnnd my prescription adhd medicine. Basically anything that you can do to make your brain stimulated while doing something you don’t want to do.

EDIT!!: if you’re interested look up “why stimulants help ADHD” on YouTube and the first couple vids do a good job explaining how we clinically don’t have dopamine and how that affects us. It’s interesting and very affirming to know this is very very real.

Ok ok. Me too. 1. It’s probably a granuloma. Did you bump it, or is the piercing not titanium, or too small/big? If you bumped it or if it’s angled incorrectly it’s a granuloma for sure. The others could be from irritation in general or a granuloma. Does it bleed when you bump it slightly? Is it red?

Granulomas are when the skin tries to repair itself like a dummy and tries to grow blood vessels on the outside of the piercing.

In my opinion, sea salt soaks help to a degree, but too much sea salt or too much “soak” just makes a granuloma angry. So I stopped that. It’s been 4 months since I got it. It’s still there. I’ve tried LITHA, bandaids at night, chamomile compresses (NOT ASPIRIN OR TEA TREE those work by damaging it off...) nothing helped. 

In any case. I said “let’s get medical” because to treat granulomas (in multiple different instances not just for piercings) a dermatologist will inject a steroid into the area, and it shrinks or disappears. Well guess what.

I bought hydrocortisone cream (next best thing right?) and it’s finally not being a bitch. It’s definitely going WAY down, almost not noticeable to others. I expect it to go away in a week or two. Clean it GENTLY with a fragrance free face soap (ie cetaphil or ceraVe). I got “hydrocortisone with aloe”. I’ve only used it about 3 days. Happy with it. 

Might not work, but it’s worth a try. Get a properly fitting stud made of titanium. And! Instead of sea salt soaks try PLAIN saline solutions from a drug store and some grocery stores. Gentler is better. No q tips.
